readerTitle: Same boss, same style, opposite results
caseNote: 가상 사례 2개 (주택 리모델링 회사, B2B 기장 대행 회사, 마케팅 에이전시) + 실제 연구 (Hersey & Blanchard, Goleman 2000)
insight: 리더십 스타일은 내 성격이 아니라 상대가 '이 일'에 대해 가진 실력과 자신감에 맞춰 고르는 것이다. 같은 사람에게도 일마다 다르게 이끈다.
misconception: 좋은 리더는 한결같은 스타일을 가지고 있고, 모두를 똑같이 대하는 것이 공정하다.

sources.text: Hersey, P. & Blanchard, K. (1969). Life Cycle Theory of Leadership. Training and Development Journal.
Goleman, D. (2000). Leadership That Gets Results. Harvard Business Review, March–April 2000.
Maria, Dev, 전기 기사, 계정 매니저 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Goleman(2000)은 Hay/McBer 컨설팅의 약 3,871명 임원 데이터를 근거로 여러 스타일을 상황에 맞게 쓰는 리더가 조직 분위기와 성과가 가장 좋았다고 보고했습니다. 표본 수는 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 "several thousand executives"로만 적었습니다.
상황적 리더십(Situational Leadership)은 상표로 등록된 이름이므로 카드 본문에서는 프레임워크 이름 대신 원리(지시와 지원의 조합)만 설명했습니다. 네 가지 조합의 영어 이름(Direct, Coach, Support, Delegate)은 일반 용어로 썼습니다.
상황적 리더십 모델의 실증 근거가 엇갈린다는 점(예: Thompson & Vecchio 2009 등 검증 연구)을 7번 카드에 일반적으로 적었습니다. 게시 전 대표 검증 연구를 한 편 확인해 sources에 추가할지 검토하세요.

cards.title: Same boss, same style, opposite results
body: Maria runs a home renovation company. She checks every job, every day. Her best carpenters keep quitting.
Dev runs a bookkeeping firm for small companies. He trusts his people and leaves them alone. His new hires keep missing deadlines.
Two opposite styles. One shared mistake: each of them leads everyone the same way.

image.label: Two managers, one hovering, one absent
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽: 공사 현장에서 숙련 목수 어깨 너머로 클립보드를 든 사장이 바짝 붙어 있고 목수는 지친 표정. 오른쪽: 사무실에서 서류 더미에 파묻힌 신입 직원, 사장 자리는 비어 있고 문에 "Back later" 메모. 실제 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: An expert who has never done this part
body: You run a home renovation company. You hire an electrician with ten years of experience. He's excellent with wiring.
But in your firm, crew leads also write price quotes for customers. He has never written one. How do you lead him on quotes?

options.text: Leave him alone. He's a pro and will figure it out
options.feedback: You show trust, but his skill is in wiring, not quoting. A few underpriced jobs could cost more than the time you saved.

options.text: Write the first quotes with him step by step, then step back as he gets it right
options.feedback: You spend time up front and give him clear direction where he's new. As his quotes improve, you hand over control.

options.text: Give him your quoting guide and review his numbers once a month
options.feedback: The guide helps, but a month is a long time for mistakes to pile up. A new skill needs faster feedback at first.

cards.title: Both bosses fixed the wrong thing.
body: Maria's veteran carpenters didn't need daily checks. To them, close watching said *I don't trust you*. So they left for firms that let them work.
Dev's new hires didn't need freedom yet. They needed clear steps, examples and quick feedback. Left alone, they guessed, and their guesses were often wrong.
Each boss used the style that felt natural to *them*. Neither asked what the other person needed.

cards.title: Adapting your style
body: **Adapting your style** means changing how much you direct and how much you support, based on a person's skill and confidence for a specific task.
Direction is telling what to do and how. Support is listening, encouraging and involving people in decisions. Mix them and you get four basic modes:
list: **Direct:** new and unsure. Clear steps, close check-ins
**Coach:** learning but shaky. Explain why, keep guiding
**Support:** skilled but hesitant. Listen, back them
**Delegate:** skilled and confident. Agree on the goal, step away

image.label: Two-by-two grid of direction and support
image.brief: 2x2 매트릭스 인포그래픽. 가로축 "Support", 세로축 "Direction". 네 칸에 "Direct", "Coach", "Support", "Delegate". 바깥에 사람 아이콘이 신입에서 숙련자로 이동하는 화살표가 칸을 따라 돈다.

cards.title: The best leaders switch.
body: The idea that style should match the follower goes back to work by Paul Hersey and Ken Blanchard in the late 1960s.

In 2000, Daniel Goleman reported in Harvard Business Review on data from several thousand executives. He described six distinct leadership styles. Leaders who moved between several of them, depending on the situation, had **better team climate and results** than leaders who relied on one.
His comparison: a golfer picks a different club for each shot.

cards.title: Match the task, not the person.
body: The electrician is a *delegate* person for wiring and a *direct* person for quotes. Same man, same week, two styles. Labeling someone "senior" or "junior" misses this.
People also move. A good leader starts close on a new task and steps back as skill grows. The goal is for people to need less of you over time.
cards.softwareNote: This often shows up when a strong engineer becomes a team lead. Leave her alone on code, but guide her closely on her first hires and her first hard conversations.

cards.title: Adapting is not being random.
body: Your style can change. Your standards and values should not. If you're strict with one person and easy on another for the same mistake, people will see favoritism, not flexibility.
Say why you're shifting: *"You're new to quoting, so I'll stay close for a few weeks."* That keeps it from feeling like distrust.
And treat the four modes as a starting point, not a law. Tests of specific style models have shown mixed results.

cards.title: A star who lost her nerve
body: You run a B2B marketing agency. Your best account manager has led pitches for years. Last month she lost your biggest client, and since then she keeps asking you to approve small decisions.
A new pitch is due in two weeks. How do you lead her?

options.text: Take over the pitch yourself so nothing goes wrong
options.feedback: You protect this pitch, but you tell her you've lost faith. Her confidence drops further, and you become the bottleneck.

options.text: Give her a detailed checklist and review every step
options.feedback: Structure can calm nerves, but her skill hasn't gone anywhere. Close direction may feel like a demotion.

options.text: Talk through what happened, then let her lead with you as a sounding board
options.feedback: Her skill is high and her confidence is low, so she needs support more than direction. You give a bit of your time and keep a strong pitcher.

cards.title: Lead the person in front of you, on the task in front of them.
body: Ask two questions before you step in: how skilled is this person at *this* task, and how confident are they? Then pick how much to direct and how much to support.
**Try it today:** list three people you work with and one task each. For each, write which mode they need now: direct, coach, support or delegate. Is it the one you're using?
